name: Joan of Arc
info: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) was a French peasant's daughter who, claiming divine guidance, helped raise the siege of Orléans and secure the coronation of Charles VII during the Hundred Years' War, and was burned for heresy at Rouen.

facts.born: c. 1412 (date unknown) in Domrémy, in the Meuse valley in north-east France; daughter of Jacques d'Arc, a peasant farmer and village official, and Isabelle Romée
facts.died: 30 May 1431 in Rouen, burned at the stake in the Vieux-Marché as a relapsed heretic, aged about nineteen; her remains were thrown into the Seine
facts.role: Military leader with the Armagnac armies of Charles VII (1429–1430), without formal command; ennobled with her family by Charles in 1429; canonized in 1920 and declared a patron saint of France in 1922
facts.known: the relief of Orléans in May 1429; the Loire Campaign and the victory at Patay; the coronation of Charles VII at Reims; her visions of Saint Michael, Saint Margaret and Saint Catherine; her trial for heresy and execution at Rouen; the rehabilitation trial of 1455–1456; her canonization in 1920

t: A peasant's daughter from Domrémy who testified that visions of saints had told her to help the Dauphin Charles, Joan reached his court at Chinon in 1429, aged seventeen.

Within months the siege of Orléans was lifted, the English army was routed at Patay and Charles was consecrated at Reims; the failures at Paris and La-Charité-sur-Loire then reduced the court's faith in her.
Captured at Compiègne in 1430 and handed to the English for a ransom, she was tried for heresy and burned at Rouen in 1431; the verdict was nullified in 1456 and she was canonized in 1920.
dyk: Joan may never have heard herself called "Jeanne d'Arc": the first written record of that name dates from 1455, 24 years after her death. In her letters she called herself Jeanne la Pucelle, "Joan the Maiden".
ev: Born in Domrémy, in the Meuse valley, to Jacques d'Arc, a peasant farmer, and Isabelle Romée
By her later testimony has her first vision, at thirteen, of a figure she identified as Saint Michael
Asks Robert de Baudricourt, garrison commander at Vaucouleurs, for an armed escort to the Armagnac court at Chinon and is refused
Arrives at Orléans in April; the English abandon the siege in May, and in July Charles VII is consecrated at Reims with Joan in a place of honour
Captured by Burgundian troops outside Compiègne and transferred to the English, who pay 10,000 livres tournois for her
Tried for heresy at Rouen, judged a relapsed heretic and burned at the stake
The rehabilitation trial finds the original trial unjust and deceitful and nullifies her abjuration and execution

sections.early:
Joan of Arc was born c. 1412 in Domrémy, a small village in the Meuse valley in the north-east of France; her date of birth is unknown, and her own statements about her age were vague. Her parents were Jacques d'Arc and Isabelle Romée. Her father was a peasant farmer with about 20 hectares of land who also served as a village official, collecting taxes and heading the local watch. Joan did household chores, spun wool, helped in the fields and looked after the animals; her mother provided her religious education, and she was not taught to read and write.

She was born during the Hundred Years' War between England and France, which had begun in 1337. France was divided between the Armagnacs and the Burgundians, and after the Duke of Burgundy was assassinated by the Dauphin's partisans in 1419 the new duke, Philip the Good, allied with the English. The Treaty of Troyes effectively disinherited the Dauphin, the future Charles VII. When Henry V of England and Charles VI of France died in 1422, the infant Henry VI was the nominal heir to both crowns, but the Dauphin also claimed the French throne.

Domrémy was surrounded by pro-Burgundian lands, but its people were loyal to the Armagnac cause. In 1425 the village was attacked and cattle were stolen. Joan later testified that at thirteen, c. 1425, a figure she identified as Saint Michael, surrounded by angels, appeared to her in the garden. Her visions, which she said came frequently, also included Saint Margaret and Saint Catherine, and she testified that she swore a vow of virginity to these voices.
sections.rise:
In May 1428 Joan asked her uncle to take her to the nearby town of Vaucouleurs, where she petitioned the garrison commander, Robert de Baudricourt, for an armed escort to the Armagnac court at Chinon. He harshly refused and sent her home. In July Burgundian forces raided Domrémy, setting fire to the town and forcing its people to flee, and the English started to surround Orléans, the last obstacle to an assault on the rest of Charles's territory. Joan returned to Vaucouleurs in January 1429 and was refused again, but she gained the support of two of Baudricourt's soldiers, Jean de Metz and Bertrand de Poulengy. After a third meeting in February, Baudricourt let her go. She travelled with an escort of six soldiers, wearing men's clothes, as she did for the rest of her life.

She met Charles at Chinon in late February or early March 1429, when she was seventeen and he was twenty-six, and told him that she had come to raise the siege of Orléans and lead him to Reims for his coronation. Charles and his council sent her to Poitiers, where a council of theologians declared her a good person and a good Catholic; they gave no decision on the source of her inspiration but agreed that sending her to Orléans would test it.

Reassured, the Dauphin commissioned plate armour for her. She designed her own banner, had a sword brought from under the altar of the church at Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, and dictated a letter to the Duke of Bedford warning that she was sent by God to drive him out of France.
sections.deeds:
Joan reached Orléans on 29 April 1429 with an army carrying supplies. She was at first treated as a figurehead to raise morale, with no formal command and no place in military councils, but she quickly gained the support of the troops, and the commanders sometimes accepted her advice on what position to attack and how to place artillery. On 4 May her appearance rallied retreating soldiers, who took the fortress of Saint-Loup. On 7 May, during the attack on the main English stronghold, les Tourelles, she was wounded by an arrow between the neck and shoulder but returned to encourage the final assault. The English retreated on 8 May, nine days after her arrival; many took the lifting of the siege as the sign she had promised.

She then insisted on a prompt advance towards Reims. With John II, Duke of Alençon, who regularly heeded her advice, she helped clear the Loire towns: Jargeau was taken by assault, and many of the English who surrendered there were killed; the garrison at Beaugency surrendered on 18 June. That day, at her urging, the Armagnacs pursued the retreating English army and routed it at the Battle of Patay; Joan arrived too late to take part in the decisive action.

The army left Gien on 29 June, and the advance was nearly unopposed; only Troyes resisted, and it negotiated a surrender once Joan directed preparations for an assault. Reims opened its gates on 16 July 1429, and Charles was consecrated the following morning, with Joan given a place of honour. At the end of December she learned that Charles had ennobled her and her family.
sections.opponents:
After the consecration Joan and Alençon favoured a quick march on Paris, but the court was negotiating with the Duke of Burgundy and advanced slowly. The assault on Paris on 8 September 1429 failed: Joan was wounded in the leg by a crossbow bolt, the Armagnacs suffered 1,500 casualties, and Charles ordered an end to the attack the next morning. Her aggressive independence did not agree with the court's emphasis on a diplomatic solution, and scholars at the University of Paris argued that she failed because her inspiration was not divine. The failure to take La-Charité-sur-Loire further diminished her reputation. At Lagny-sur-Marne in 1430 she allowed the townspeople to execute the captured mercenary Franquet d'Arras after a trial.

The English saw a peasant girl's ability to defeat their armies as proof that she was possessed by the devil. At Rouen she was accused of blaspheming by wearing men's clothes, of acting upon demonic visions, and of refusing to submit her words and deeds to the church. The trial was politically motivated: her guilt could be used to show that Charles had been consecrated by the act of a heretic. Bishop Pierre Cauchon of Beauvais, a partisan of the Duke of Burgundy and the English crown, was the judge, and the English subsidized the trial.

Modern scholars have discussed neurological and psychiatric causes for her visions, among them epilepsy and schizophrenia; many of these explanations have been challenged, since the trial records are unlikely to provide the objective descriptions a diagnosis needs.
sections.last:
During the truce with Burgundy the court had no need for Joan. At the end of March 1430 she set out with a company of volunteers to relieve Compiègne, without the explicit permission of Charles. She reached the town on 14 May. On 23 May she joined a sortie against the Burgundian camp at Margny; the attack failed and she surrendered to Lyonnel de Wandomme, of Jean de Luxembourg's contingent. She tried twice to escape, the second time jumping from a tower window at Beaurevoir Castle into a dry moat. The English paid 10,000 livres tournois to obtain her and moved her to Rouen. There is no evidence that Charles tried to save her.

Her trial for heresy opened on 9 January 1431. It had many irregularities: she was imprisoned by the English and guarded by male soldiers instead of being held by the church and guarded by women, she was interrogated at length without legal counsel, and there is evidence that the records were falsified. On 24 May, in the churchyard of the abbey of Saint-Ouen, as Cauchon began to read her sentence, she agreed to submit and signed an abjuration. She was returned to her cell in chains. Witnesses later stated that she was subjected to mistreatment and rape attempts and that guards placed men's clothes in her cell. On 28 May she told Cauchon that her voices had blamed her for abjuring out of fear and that she would not deny them again.

The assessors voted unanimously that she was a relapsed heretic. On 30 May 1431, aged about nineteen, she was burned in Rouen's Vieux-Marché, a crucifix held before her eyes. Her remains were thrown into the Seine.
sections.legacy:
Her execution did not change the military situation: the English could not regain momentum, and the war ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453. Because the verdict implied that Charles owed his consecration to a heretic, he ordered an inquest in 1450. A rehabilitation trial permitted by Pope Callixtus III opened on 7 November 1455 with a formal request from Joan's mother and ended on 7 July 1456, having heard about 115 witnesses. It found the original trial unjust and deceitful and nullified the sentence, though it did not declare her visions authentic.

Orléans celebrated the raising of the siege on 8 May from as early as 1429, and the festival continues. During the French Revolution her association with monarchy and religion brought her reputation into question, and the festival was suspended in 1793; Napoleon Bonaparte authorized its renewal in 1803. Since then she has been a symbol of the French nation used across the political spectrum: in the Second World War by Philippe Pétain in Vichy France, by Charles de Gaulle's Free French and by the Communist resistance, and more recently by the far right.

She was beatified by Pope Pius X in 1909 and canonized on 16 May 1920 by Pope Benedict XV, as a virgin rather than a martyr, because a canonically constituted court had put her to death; she has nevertheless been popularly venerated as a martyr. In 1922 Pope Pius XI declared her one of the patron saints of France. She has also been described as a protofeminist and as a model of an autonomous woman.

summary: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431), a peasant's daughter from Domrémy, said that visions of saints sent her to help Charles VII. She took part in the relief of Orléans and saw him consecrated at Reims in 1429, was captured in 1430 and burned for heresy at Rouen. The verdict was nullified in 1456, and she was canonized in 1920.

notes: Birth: the article gives only 'c. 1412' and says the date is unknown; start 1412, circa true.
The article's lead says she was 'about seventeen' when sent to Orléans; the Chinon section says 'she was seventeen and he was twenty-six'. Used as given in each place.
The lead says Benedict XV canonized her in 1920 'and, two years later, was declared one of the patron saints'; the Legacy section names Pius XI for 1922. The section follows the Legacy section.
The article calls Henry VI 9 months old in 1422 and 'ten-year-old' at his Paris coronation in 1431; only 'infant' in 1422 is used.
The article gives no year for the Treaty of Troyes, so none is given.
The transfer to the English: negotiations 'were completed in November' (1430); the lead says 'handed to the English in November'. The event keeps capture and transfer together under 1430.
The 1429 event joins Orléans (April-May) and the consecration at Reims (July) to stay within eight events.
Spelling follows British usage outside quotations (armour, honour, favoured); the article is in American spelling.
Ennoblement: the article says she learned of it on returning to court 'at the end of December' (1429 by context); the role fact says 1429.

Left out for space: the prophecies of Marie Robine and Merlin, the visit to the Duke of Lorraine, the 'God's grace' answer at the trial, the vote on torture, details of her clothing and Aquinas's and Gerson's views on it, the inquests of 1450 and 1452 in detail, Leo XIII's 1894 pronouncement, the Church of England commemoration and Cao Dai.

'Opponents' cites only two of the proposed diagnoses (epilepsy, schizophrenia); the article lists more (temporal lobe tuberculoma, ergot poisoning, delusional disorder, creative psychopathy, hysteria).
